intro: Lesson 2: 'Your country needs you!': recruitment and propaganda. To understand how Britain recruited soldiers and used propaganda in the First World War

model.title: How does a recruitment poster persuade?

parts.label: Step 1
parts.text: Who made it: the government or a supporter

parts.label: Step 4
parts.text: What it leaves out: the danger and the dead

parts.label: Answer
parts.text: It persuades through emotion and leaves out the cost of war.

questions.q: Give three reasons men volunteered in 1914.
questions.a: For example: duty to defend Belgium and Britain, joining with friends, wages and adventure
questions.model: One from each column: Duty: defend Belgium. Pressure: posters and shaming. Personal: join with friends. That gives three reasons.

questions.q: Why did the government censor news?
questions.a: To keep up morale and recruitment by hiding bad news
Not enough men were volunteering after heavy losses

questions.q: Core: In the portal response box, write a PEEL paragraph: 'The main reason men volunteered in 1914 was ...'
questions.a: A clear point with evidence (for example, Pals battalions, Kitchener's call, Belgium) and explanation
questions.model: Teacher goes through it first: 'The main reason was a sense of duty (P). Germany had invaded Belgium, and Kitchener called for volunteers (E). Men believed defending their country was right (E). So duty explains the rush to join (L).'

questions.q: Extend: How reliable are recruitment posters as evidence of why men joined?
questions.a: They show what the government wanted men to feel, not what men actually felt

questions.q: Stretch: Should conscientious objectors have been punished? Give a view.
questions.a: Reasoned view on freedom of belief versus national need

questions.q: Big question: why did so many young men volunteer to fight in 1914?
questions.a: Duty, propaganda and social pressure, friends joining together, wages and the belief it would be short
